title: India & South Asia: GI Spirits and Traditional Ferments
attribution: South Asia's drinks span a protected geographical indication (Goa's Feni) and a vast body of tribal and rural ferments with no statutory definition, documented from ethnographic and food-science sources. Feni figures follow the Goa GI specification; the traditional entries give typical values and are marked as customary rather than regulated.

styles.name: Cashew Feni (काजू फेणी, GI)
styles.impression: Goa's protected spirit: pungent, fruity and sulphurous, double-distilled from the fermented juice of the cashew apple.
styles.comments: Registered geographical indication (GI No. 120, 2009). Traditionally distilled in earthenware bhann pots. Urrak is a seasonal low-strength drink in its own right.
styles.ingredients: Cashew apples (the false fruit), crushed and fermented, then twice pot-distilled. First distillation gives urrak (~15%); the second gives feni.
styles.tags: india, goa, feni, cashew, GI, spirit

styles.name: Coconut / Toddy Feni
styles.impression: The palm-sap version of feni: softer and more vegetal than cashew, distilled from fermented coconut toddy.
styles.comments: Also covered by the Goa GI. The older of the two feni traditions in coastal Goa.
styles.tags: india, goa, feni, coconut, toddy, GI

styles.name: Toddy / Tadi / Kallu (ताड़ी)
styles.impression: Fresh-tapped palm sap that ferments within hours — sweet and mild in the morning, sharp and sour by afternoon, mildly alcoholic and fizzy.
styles.comments: Drunk across South and coastal India and the world's palm belt. Distilled it becomes arrack. Unstable — consumed the day it is tapped.
styles.ingredients: Sap of coconut, palmyra or date palm, collected in pots on the tree; wild yeast begins fermenting immediately.

styles.name: Mahua (महुआ)
styles.impression: A tribal spirit distilled from the sweet, heady flowers of the mahua tree — earthy, floral and fiery.
styles.comments: Central to Adivasi (tribal) culture across central India; long stigmatised and restricted, now being reframed as a heritage craft spirit. The flowers are also a food.
styles.ingredients: Dried mahua (Madhuca longifolia) flowers, fermented and pot-distilled.

categories.name: Rice & Grain Beers of the Northeast & Himalaya

styles.name: Handia / Apong (हंडिया / अपong)
styles.impression: Tribal rice beer of eastern and northeastern India — cloudy, sour-sweet and lightly alcoholic, brewed with a herbal starter cake.
styles.comments: Handia among the Santal and other central tribes; apong among the Mising and other Assamese communities. Both social and ritual drinks.
styles.ingredients: Cooked rice mixed with a starter (ranu/bakhar/emao) of ground herbs and wild moulds/yeasts, fermented in earthen pots.

styles.name: Chhaang (छ्याङ)
styles.impression: Himalayan fermented-grain beer, drunk warm in the cold — milky, sour and warming, sometimes sipped through a bamboo straw from the fermenting vessel.
styles.comments: Drunk across Nepal, Sikkim, Bhutan and Tibet. Tongba is the millet, straw-sipped variant.
styles.ingredients: Barley, millet or rice fermented with a starter; in the tongba form, hot water is repeatedly poured over fermented millet in a wooden vessel.
